_meta.scope: 11 base patterns base_p0..base_p10; 3-judge panel {gpt52, claude_opus, claude_sonnet}; satisfied_is_known only
_meta.tools: factor_analyzer 0.5.1 (EFA minres + promax oblique + Horn parallel analysis); sentence-transformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (local/offline); sklearn KMeans; TF-IDF
caveats_global: df_verdicts has satisfied_is_known==True for every row here (no unknown verdicts to drop).

Marginalising the 3 judges by averaging DISATTENUATES dimension correlations and inflates the general factor => 1-factor solutions; single-judge solutions preserve item covariance and reveal >=2 factors. Both are reported.
Criterion-level FA uses Pearson correlations on binary items (tetrachoric would be preferable but factor_analyzer's parallel analysis path is Pearson-based).

Judge free-text is templated on the criterion wording, so high-purity clusters largely recover criterion identity; the CROSS-DIMENSION themes are the informative, non-trivial output and are stable across k=15/20/25.

factor_model.question: Is 'report quality' ONE latent construct, or >=2 orthogonal factors (a 'form' factor = analytical_depth/organization/citation vs a 'truth' factor = factual_accuracy/attribution)?
factor_model.method: EFA (minres extraction) with promax OBLIQUE rotation (so inter-factor correlation phi is estimable) + Horn parallel analysis (1000 sims) for #factors; Kaiser>1 reported alongside. Primary unit = report x 9 dimension scores (met/total); robustness unit = report x 38 general binary criteria.
factor_model.adequacy: KMO 0.78-0.93, Bartlett p<1e-300 across solutions => data are factorable.

key_numbers.crit_opus_truth_sourcing_factor: factual_accuracy+citation_quality+attribution_quality -> one factor; phi to content bulk = 0.453

factor_model.verdict: NOT a clean single construct. A dominant general-quality factor exists, but a SEPARABLE second factor anchored by the sourcing/truth dimensions (factual_accuracy + citation_quality + attribution_quality) recurs in 2 of 3 single-judge solutions AND in the criterion-level solutions. Its correlation with the 'form/content' factor is weak-to-moderate and judge-dependent: r=0.108 (gpt52, near-orthogonal form vs truth), 0.453 (opus criterion-level), 0.553 (opus dimension-level). attribution_quality is the single most consistent outlier (lowest communality 0.217 and lowest loading 0.466 even in the disattenuated 1-factor solution). sonnet is the exception (unidimensional). Whether you 'see' 1 vs >=2 factors is driven by (a) judge and (b) averaging: averaging the panel inflates the general factor.
factor_model.supports_bounded_returns: YES, with caveats. When judge idiosyncrasy is preserved (gpt52), 'form' (organization/depth/citation) and 'truth' (factual_accuracy) sit on near-orthogonal factors (r=0.11 < 0.5). Orchestration that lifts the form factor need not move the weakly-coupled truth/sourcing factor => a factor-analytic mechanism for bounded returns and a caution against single-score leaderboards for the sourcing/factual dimensions.
factor_model.paper_statement: An exploratory factor analysis with parallel analysis over the 11-pattern x 3-judge verdict tensor finds that report quality is not a single latent construct: alongside a dominant general-quality factor, a separable 'sourcing/truth' factor anchored by factual_accuracy, citation_quality and attribution_quality recurs across the single-judge and criterion-level solutions, with attribution_quality the most consistent outlier (communality 0.22 even in the pooled one-factor fit). Its correlation with the 'form/content' factor is weak and judge-dependent - near-orthogonal under the GPT-5.2 judge (r=0.11) and only moderate under Claude Opus (r=0.45-0.55) - so a report can score highly on analytical depth, organisation and citation form while remaining flat on factual and attribution quality. This supplies a factor-analytic mechanism for bounded returns to orchestration and a caution against collapsing these weakly-coupled axes into one leaderboard number (the apparent unidimensionality of the pooled panel is partly an artefact of averaging judges, which disattenuates the inter-dimension correlations).

fail_reason_clusters.method: NOT-satisfied verdicts (satisfied==0) for 11 base patterns x 3-judge, reasoning>=15 chars; embedded with local all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384-d, cosine-normalised, offline); KMeans at k=15/20/25 (primary k=20); representative terms via cluster-mean TF-IDF (1-2 grams), representative reasoning via nearest-to-centroid; dimension purity + normalised entropy per cluster; CROSS-DIMENSION flag = purity<0.45 AND >=3 dimensions each >=10%.

fail_reason_clusters.verdict: Most fail clusters are criterion-anchored (judge reasoning echoes the criterion wording -> high purity, e.g. 'author-analysis vs sourced material' 0.97, 'traceable to named sources' 0.90, 'citation formatting inconsistent' 0.97, 'multiple perspectives/schools of thought' 0.95, 'causal arguments unsupported' 0.94). BUT five stable CROSS-DIMENSION themes emerge that map to NO single rubric dimension and together account for ~42% of all fails: (1) temporal currency/staleness, (2) epistemic calibration/uncertainty-signalling, (3) descriptive-vs-mechanistic depth & practical trade-offs, (4) placeholder/non-specific sources, (5) question-answering decisiveness. A sixth max-entropy cluster is a degenerate 'no content' artefact (76% base_p9). Themes 1-5 are candidate UNDISCOVERED quality axes; the current 9-dimension rubric splits each of them across 3-4 dimensions, which both dilutes their signal and helps explain why single-dimension scores move less than the underlying failure would suggest.
fail_reason_clusters.paper_statement: Embedding and clustering the ~46k failing verdict rationales shows that while most failure clusters simply re-express a single rubric criterion, five recurrent themes cut cleanly ACROSS dimensions and are owned by no single one: temporal staleness (report misses the current state of the art / recent developments), poor epistemic calibration (no distinction between established and contested claims, no uncertainty signalling), descriptive-rather-than-mechanistic depth (facts catalogued but trade-offs and practical implications absent), non-specific 'Web Search Synthesis' placeholder sourcing, and a failure of decisiveness in directly answering the posed question. Together these cross-dimension themes account for roughly 42% of all failing verdicts, each currently scattered across three to four rubric dimensions, suggesting the 9-dimension rubric under-resolves several genuine quality axes. A sixth, maximally cross-dimensional cluster is not a quality axis at all but a degenerate empty-output artefact concentrated (76%) in the local 7B baseline (base_p9), a data-quality flag in its own right.
